title: the sandals on the throne
hookLine: Bharata rules fourteen years with Rama's sandals on the throne
carry: touching feet is humility that asks a blessing

cards: Over Kishkindha, Sita asks Rama for something. She wants the wives of the monkey leaders, Tara and the others, to come with them to Ayodhya and share the homecoming.
So the Pushpaka comes down, and the women climb aboard in their best clothes. Rama agrees at once. The woman who spent months among strangers wants to arrive home surrounded by friends.

teach.b: Then the flight north becomes the whole story, told backward. Rama points out the places: Rishyamuka, where he met Sugriva; Panchavati, where Ravana took Sita; Chitrakuta, where Bharata came to find him.
They land at the sage Bharadvaja's hermitage on the day the fourteen years are complete, and Rama sends Hanuman ahead with a strange instruction: tell Bharata I'm coming, and watch his face.

If, after fourteen years, he wants to keep the kingdom, let him have it. Some readers hear a test; others hear respect. Hanuman finds Bharata at Nandigram, outside the capital, living like a hermit in bark clothes.
On the throne sit Rama's sandals. Years before, in the forest, Bharata begged Rama to come home, and when Rama wouldn't break his word to their father, Bharata asked for his sandals instead.
He set them on the throne and ruled as their servant. Rama is coming, Hanuman tells him, and Bharata falls to the ground with joy. Why sandals?

teach.h: THE FEET OF THE ONE YOU HONOR.
teach.b: In Hindu tradition, the feet of the one you honor are holy. They're the lowest part of a person, so bowing to them says: I make myself small before you.

That's why Hindus bow at the feet of God in the temple, why the padukas of gurus are kept and worshiped in shrines, and why children touch their elders' feet, especially on festival days, and get a blessing back.

teach.h: THE SERVANT OF A PAIR OF SANDALS.
teach.b: Bharata held a kingdom for fourteen years and called himself the servant of a pair of sandals.

how: On Diwali and other festival days, many Hindu children touch the feet of their parents and elders and receive a blessing; in many lineages a guru's padukas, sandals, are kept in the shrine and worshiped.

Hindus touch an elder's feet to ask for their blessing
the feet are the lowest part; bowing there says i make myself small, and the elder blesses back.
Bharata lived in the palace while Rama was away

games.q: on Diwali, your grandmother's sister walks in. you've barely met her. by Bharata's story, what fits?
o: wave from the couch; you don't really know her.
bow and touch her feet, or fold your hands, and take her blessing.
shake her hand like any guest.
games.why: Bharata honored his brother's sandals for fourteen years. bowing to an elder's feet is the same humility, and it asks a blessing back.

practice: Picture an elder in your life, or a teacher who shaped you. On festival days, many Hindu children bow and touch an elder's feet, and the elder blesses them.
Bow your head a little where you sit, as if you were at their feet, and silently ask for their blessing. If you don't pray, simply let one long breath carry your thanks to them.

wordCard.voice: Paduka. Sandals: Rama's, set on the throne for fourteen years while Bharata ruled as their servant.

orig.note: Sanskrit pādukā: sandals; Bharata ruled with Rama's sandals on the throne, from pāda, foot.

carryVoice: Your line: touching feet is humility that asks a blessing. Bharata lived it for fourteen years, bowing to a pair of sandals. That's day six hundred sixty-one.
